Stage 3 · Grammar

How sure are you?

Four small words that place a guess on a scale.

Read these three sentences about the same painting.
  • It must be either an old painting or a historical scene.
  • They might be going out to hunt.
  • They can’t be going out to hunt — they’ve caught something.
Which of these express certainty?
These modals do not talk about the future. They talk about how sure you are of a conclusion.

There are two quite separate jobs that must, might and can’t can do in English, and confusing them is a genuine source of misunderstanding. In Lesson 8 they expressed obligation and permission. Here they express deduction: reasoning from evidence to a conclusion about what is or was the case.

The system has three points. Must says the evidence leaves only one explanation: The river must be frozen — people are skating on it. Can’t says the evidence rules an explanation out: They can’t be going hunting — they’ve already caught something. And might, may and could sit between the two: possible, but not established.

The negative pair is where almost all errors happen, because the pattern is not the one you would predict. The opposite of It must be true is It can’t be true, not it mustn’t be true — mustn’t belongs to prohibition and has no role in this lesson at all. Equally, the negative of It might be true is It might not be true, not it couldn’t, because couldn’t means impossible and therefore belongs with can’t.

A deduction is only convincing with its evidence attached, and English speakers habitually give both in one breath: the conclusion first, then the reason, joined by because or a dash. A conclusion offered without evidence is heard as a guess. This is also the pattern you will need when you describe and interpret a painting, which is the context of this lesson.

Before you look at the table: the table below shows the three levels of certainty and then the two time frames — about now, and about the past. Learn the negative pair must be / can’t be as a single unit.
The certainty scale
How sureWordExample
Certain yesmustThe river must be frozen — people are skating on it.
Possiblemight / may / couldThey might be cooking something.
Certain nocan’tIt can’t be a window — it’s reflecting the sea.
Now, or earlier?
 About nowAbout the past
StateIt must be a mirror.It must have been painted in winter.
Action in progressThey might be cooking.They might have been cooking.
Certain noIt can’t be a window.It can’t have been easy to paint.
Patternmodal + be / be…ingmodal + have been / have been…ing

The opposite of must is can’t, not mustn’t. It must be a mirror → It can’t be a mirror. Mustn’t means “do not do it”, which is a completely different job.

No to after these modals. Not It must to be a mirror but It must be a mirror. Same for might, could and can’t.

Give the evidence. A good deduction comes with a reason attached: The river must be frozen, because people are skating on it. Without the reason it is just an opinion in a confident voice.

Changing your mind out loud is normal. Ah, no — they can’t be going out to hunt, because I can see they’ve caught something. English speakers correct themselves mid-description constantly, and it sounds fluent rather than uncertain.

Full grammar reference — deduction and speculation — must, might, could, can’t

What it is

These modals express how certain you are about a conclusion, not about a future event. Must says the evidence leaves only one explanation. Can’t says the evidence rules an explanation out. Might, may and could sit between the two: possible, but not established.

What it means, and what it does

This is the language of reasoning aloud. When you look at a painting, a photograph or a situation and work out what is happening, English expects you to mark the strength of your inference. Saying It is a mirror claims knowledge you do not have; saying It must be a mirror — it’s reflecting the sea claims a conclusion and shows the evidence behind it. That second move is what a competent B1 speaker does.

When and why we use it

There are two quite separate jobs that must, might and can’t can do in English, and confusing them is a genuine source of misunderstanding. In Lesson 8 they expressed obligation and permission. Here they express deduction: reasoning from evidence to a conclusion about what is or was the case.

The system has three points. Must says the evidence leaves only one explanation: The river must be frozen — people are skating on it. Can’t says the evidence rules an explanation out: They can’t be going hunting — they’ve already caught something. And might, may and could sit between the two: possible, but not established.

The negative pair is where almost all errors happen, because the pattern is not the one you would predict. The opposite of It must be true is It can’t be true, not it mustn’t be true — mustn’t belongs to prohibition and has no role in this lesson at all. Equally, the negative of It might be true is It might not be true, not it couldn’t, because couldn’t means impossible and therefore belongs with can’t.

A deduction is only convincing with its evidence attached, and English speakers habitually give both in one breath: the conclusion first, then the reason, joined by because or a dash. A conclusion offered without evidence is heard as a guess. This is also the pattern you will need when you describe and interpret a painting, which is the context of this lesson.

Typical situations

You need this for interpreting pictures and photographs, working out what is happening in a situation you have walked into, speculating about people’s motives, and reasoning aloud in a discussion.

  • A confident conclusion — must — the only explanation that fits.The river must be frozen, because people are skating on it.
  • Ruling something out — can’t — the evidence makes it impossible.They can’t be going out to hunt — they’ve already caught something.
  • An open possibility — might, may, could.They could be cooking something over the fire.
  • Correcting yourself mid-thought — the natural sequence of speculation.It might be a window — no, actually, it can’t be. It must be a mirror.
  • Deduction about now — must / might / can’t + be + -ing.She must be waiting for someone.
  • Deduction about the past — must / might / can’t + have + past participle.It must have been painted in winter.
  • Hedging a description — softening a claim you cannot prove.I’d say it’s probably an old painting rather than a modern one.

How it differs from similar structures

must (certain it is) → might / may / could (possible) → can’t (certain it isn’t). Three points on one scale of certainty about a conclusion.
must = deduction (He must be tired — he’s been up all night) · must = obligation (He must be here by nine). Only the context separates them, which is why the evidence clause matters.

How to build it

About now — state: subject + must / might / could / can’t + be + adjective / noun
About now — action: subject + must / might / could / can’t + be + verb-ing
About the past: subject + must / might / could / can’t + have + past participle
Evidence: conclusion + because / — + the reason
Certain positiveIt must be a mirror. · He must have money.
Certain negativeIt can’t be a window. · She can’t be his mother.
PossibleIt might be a story. · They could be cooking. · It may be a portrait.
Possible negativeIt might not be finished. — note: not couldn’t.
In progress nowShe must be waiting. · They might be leaving.
About the pastHe must have forgotten. · They can’t have seen us.
QuestionEnglish avoids these in questions; ask Do you think it’s a mirror? instead.
Short answerIt must be. · It can’t be. — the modal carries the answer.

Saying it — contractions and stress

  • must have, might have and can’t have reduce to must’ve /ˈmʌstəv/, might’ve, can’t’ve. They are commonly misheard, and then miswritten as must of.
  • must loses its t before a consonant: must be sounds like ‘mus’ be’.
  • Stress marks the certainty: It MUST be (confident) versus It might BE, I suppose (tentative).

Usage notes and exceptions

  • The negative of must here is can’t, not mustn’t. Mustn’t means ‘it is forbidden’ (Lesson 8) and has nothing to do with deduction. It can’t be true is the opposite of It must be true.
  • The negative of might is might not. Couldn’t means ‘impossible’, so it belongs with can’t, not with might.
  • May, might and could are close in meaning here; could is slightly weaker and may slightly more formal.
  • A deduction is only convincing with evidence attached. English speakers routinely say the conclusion first and the evidence second, joined by because or a dash.
  • For past deduction, the whole modal phrase steps back by adding have — the modal itself never changes: must be → must have been.
  • These modals are not normally used in questions. Use Do you think…?, Could it be…? or Is it possible that…? instead.

Watch out — the mistakes learners really make

  • It mustn’t be a window. → It can’t be a window.Mustn’t means forbidden; the negative deduction is can’t.
  • They couldn’t be cooking — maybe they are. → They might not be cooking.Couldn’t means impossible; use might not for uncertainty.
  • She must to be waiting for someone. → She must be waiting for someone.Modals take the base verb with no to.
  • It must been painted in winter. → It must have been painted in winter.Past deduction needs have + past participle.
  • He must of forgotten. → He must have forgotten.Must’ve is must have, never must of.
  • Must it be a mirror? → Do you think it’s a mirror?Deduction modals are not used in direct questions.

More examples in context

  • confident conclusionThe river must be frozen over, because people are skating on it.
  • ruling outThey can’t be going out to hunt — I can see they’ve caught something.
  • possibilityThere’s a group of women round a fire; they could be cooking.
  • possibilityIt might be a picture of an old story.
  • self-correctionBehind her there’s a curved window — no, it can’t be a window. It must be a mirror.
  • action nowShe must be waiting for the light to change.
  • past deductionIt must have been painted in the seventeenth century.
  • past deduction, negativeThey can’t have finished it in one sitting.
  • hedgedIt may well be a historical scene rather than a real place.
  • with evidenceIt must be cold: there’s snow on the ground and on the mountains.

A tip for remembering it

Build every deduction in two halves: conclusion + evidence. Say the modal first, then because and what you can actually see. And memorise the negative pair as a unit, because it is the one thing learners get wrong: must be ↔ can’t be. Mustn’t never appears in this lesson at all.

Before you practise — the key rules

  1. Must = the only possible conclusion; can’t = an impossible one; might / may / could = possible.
  2. The negative of must in deduction is can’t, never mustn’t.
  3. The negative of might is might not, never couldn’t.
  4. About now: modal + be (+ -ing). About the past: modal + have + past participle.
  5. Write must have, not must of.
  6. Always attach the evidence — a deduction without a reason is just a guess.

10a · Read the whole text first. Then choose the form that fits each gap.

We see faces where there are none. A tap, a teapot, the front of a house — if two blobs sit above a curve, the brain decides it a face. Scientists have come up with several explanations. It a side effect of how quickly we have to recognize people. It something older than that: an animal that mistook a rock for a predator lost nothing, while one that mistook a predator for a rock lost everything. Whatever the cause, the effect switched off. A German studio is building a database of houses that look like faces. Looking through it, you begin to feel that the buildings designed that way on purpose. They almost certainly . The architects that anybody would ever see it, and that exactly why the effect is so strong.
